title: Choosing displays and spotting misleading graphs
blurb: Match each kind of question to the right display, and catch truncated axes, uneven intervals, picture distortions, cherry-picked windows and bad pie totals.
question: A health department flyer shows Clinic A's vaccination rate (92%) with a bar three times as tall as Clinic B's (88%). The vertical axis starts at 86%. What is the real difference between the clinics, and why does the graph exaggerate it?

teach.body: Formally, a data display should match the type of data and the question being asked, and its scale must represent values proportionally. In plain English: pick the graph that answers the question (change over time, comparing groups, shares of a whole, spread, or a relationship), and then check that the picture isn't stretching the truth. The numbers on a misleading graph can be perfectly accurate while the picture lies.

teach.h: Match the question to the display
head: If the question is...
Best display
rows: How did it change over time?
What share of the whole is each part?
How are one variable's numbers spread?

items: Tanya Brooks, a nursing applicant, is making a poster with five data sets.
Monthly flu cases for 2 years: change over time, so a line graph.
Volunteers from each of 4 colleges: comparing categories, so a bar graph. How the fair's $3,000 budget was split: parts of a whole, so a pie chart.
Ages of 120 attendees: spread of one numeric variable, so a histogram. Attendees' weight vs blood pressure: two numeric variables, so a scatterplot.

teach.caption: Measured from 86%, A's bar is 6 units tall and B's is 2, so A looks 3 times as high.
Same data from 0%: the bars are nearly equal, which is the truth.

teach.h: Worked example: how big is the distortion?
items: Visible heights on the truncated axis: 92 − 86 = 6 and 88 − 86 = 2. A's bar looks 6 ÷ 2 = 3 times as tall.
As a percent of B's rate: 4 ÷ 88 = 0.045, so A is about 4.5% higher. Check: 88 × 1.045 = 91.96 ≈ 92. ✓
Lesson: on a truncated axis, compare the NUMBERS, not the bar heights.

teach.h: Four more ways a graph can mislead
teach.body: Uneven intervals: axis labels like 2000, 2010, 2020, 2021 placed equally far apart squeeze ten years into the same width as one. Picture graphs: doubling a picture's height AND width makes its area 4 times bigger, so a doubling looks like quadrupling. Cherry-picked windows: showing only the months that rose. Bad pie charts: slices that add to more or less than 100%. Also watch for missing labels or units.

teach.h: Cherry-picking: one year of monthly ER visits
teach.caption: A report showing only March to June claims visits are 'surging' (up 60). The full year ends 10 visits LOWER than it began.

teach.h: Five questions to ask any graph

steps.label: Does the axis start at 0?
steps.sub: If not, compare numbers, not heights

steps.label: Are intervals even?
steps.sub: Equal spacing should mean equal steps

steps.label: Do parts add to 100%?
steps.sub: And are labels and units shown?

teach.text: Classic slips: judging the size of a difference by bar heights on an axis that doesn't start at 0; reading equally spaced but uneven dates as equal time steps; and choosing a line graph for categories that aren't in time order, or a pie chart for data that aren't parts of one whole.

items: Line = change over time; bar = compare categories; pie = parts of a whole; histogram = spread of one numeric variable; scatterplot = relationship between two.
Truncated axis: visible height = value − axis start; compare the actual values.
Doubling both dimensions of a picture quadruples its area.
Check intervals, time windows and pie totals (100%).

summary: You can now choose the right display for any data question and spot the five classic distortions: truncated axes, uneven intervals, scaled pictures, cherry-picked time windows and pie charts that don't total 100%. You can also calculate how much a truncated axis exaggerates a difference.

A.q: A nurse manager wants to show how the number of patient falls on a unit changed from month to month over two years. Which display is most appropriate?
A.why: Change over time is shown best by a line graph, with months on the x-axis and falls on the y-axis.

whyNot.0: A pie chart shows parts of one whole, not change over time.
whyNot.1: A histogram shows how one numeric variable is spread across intervals, not a time sequence.
whyNot.3: A scatterplot shows whether two numeric variables are related, not a trend through time.

A.q: A bar graph of patient satisfaction has a vertical axis that starts at 80%. Hospital A's bar reaches 95% and Hospital B's reaches 85%, so A's bar looks 3 times as tall. Which statement is correct?
options: A is 10 percentage points higher than B
A's rate is 3 times as high as B's rate
A is 15 percentage points higher than B
A is 5 percentage points higher than B
A.why: Compare the actual values, not the bar heights: 95% − 85% = 10 percentage points. The truncated axis makes A's bar (15 units above 80) look 3 times B's (5 units).

whyNot.1: 3 times is the ratio of the visible heights (15 ÷ 5), created by starting the axis at 80%.
whyNot.2: 15 is A's visible height above 80%, not the difference between the hospitals.
whyNot.3: 5 is B's visible height above 80%, not the difference between the hospitals.

A.q: A pharmacy's pictograph shows a pill bottle for 2023 sales. For 2024, when sales doubled, the artist drew the bottle twice as tall and twice as wide. Why is this misleading?
options: Its height should be 4 times as large
Its area is 4 times as large as before
Its area is 2 times as large as before
Its width should be 4 times as large
A.why: Area = height × width, so doubling both makes the picture 2 × 2 = 4 times as big. The eye reads area, so sales appear to have quadrupled when they only doubled.

whyNot.0: A 4-times-taller bottle would exaggerate even more; to show doubling, the area should double.
whyNot.2: Doubling both dimensions gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the area, not 2 times.
whyNot.3: Making the width 4 times larger would also show the wrong amount; the area should only double.

B.q: A clinic's flyer graphs flu vaccinations only from October to December, showing a 40% rise, under the headline 'Vaccinations are soaring.' The clinic's annual total actually fell 5%. What is the main flaw in the graph?
B.why: Showing only the three months that rose, while the full year fell, is a cherry-picked time window.

whyNot.0: A truncated axis exaggerates differences in height; the problem here is which months were shown.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests the months were unevenly spaced; the issue is the months left out.
whyNot.3: Adding to 100% applies to pie charts, not to a graph of vaccinations over time.

B.q: A pie chart of a hospital's spending has four slices labeled Salaries 45%, Supplies 30%, Equipment 20% and Facilities 15%. Which statement about the chart is correct?
B.why: 45 + 30 + 20 + 15 = 110%. A pie chart's slices must total 100%, so at least one label is wrong.

whyNot.2: The labels add to 110%, which is exactly what makes the chart wrong.

B.q: A nursing program wants to show how the cholesterol levels of 200 patients are spread across ranges such as 140–159, 160–179 and 180–199 mg/dL. Which display is most appropriate?
B.why: The spread of one numeric variable across touching intervals is shown by a histogram.

whyNot.0: A bar graph compares separate categories; cholesterol ranges are continuous numeric intervals, which a histogram shows.
whyNot.1: A line graph shows change over time, not how values are spread.
whyNot.3: A pie chart shows shares of a whole, not the shape of a numeric distribution.

C.q: A line graph's x-axis labels 2000, 2010, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2023 at equal spacing. The line rises by about the same height in every segment. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Yearly growth was the same in every segment
Yearly growth was about 10 times faster before 2020
Yearly growth slowed down sharply after 2020
Yearly growth was about 10 times faster after 2020
C.why: Before 2020 each segment covers 10 years; after 2020 each covers 1 year. The same rise in one-tenth of the time means the yearly growth was about 10 times faster after 2020.

whyNot.0: Equal-looking segments hide unequal time spans: 10 years each before 2020 and 1 year each after.
whyNot.1: The same rise spread over 10 years is SLOWER per year, so growth before 2020 was about one-tenth as fast.
whyNot.2: After 2020 the same rise happens in 1 year instead of 10, so yearly growth sped up rather than slowed.

C.q: A news graphic shows average ER waits of 48 minutes at City Hospital and 40 minutes at County Hospital, with the vertical axis starting at 36 minutes. Which statement is correct?
C.why: Actual: (48 − 40) ÷ 40 = 8 ÷ 40 = 0.2, so City's wait is 20% longer. Visible heights: 48 − 36 = 12 and 40 − 36 = 4, so City's bar looks 12 ÷ 4 = 3 times as tall.

whyNot.1: 1.2 times is how the bars would compare on an axis starting at 0, not on this truncated one.
whyNot.2: 8 is the difference in minutes, not a percent; 8 ÷ 40 = 20%.
whyNot.3: 300% treats the distorted bar heights as the real comparison (and even 3 times as tall would be 200% more, not 300%).

C.q: A researcher has, for 150 adults, the average hours of sleep per night and the number of sick days taken in a year. Which display best shows whether more sleep goes with fewer sick days?
C.why: Two numeric variables measured on the same people are shown with a scatterplot, which reveals any correlation between them.

whyNot.0: A line graph tracks one variable over time; connecting 150 different people's points in order would be meaningless.
whyNot.1: A histogram shows the spread of ONE variable, so it can't show a relationship between two.
whyNot.2: A circle (pie) graph shows parts of a whole, not a relationship.

reteach.title: The funhouse mirror
reteach.question: A funhouse mirror shows the real you, just stretched. How is a misleading graph like a funhouse mirror?

blocks.body: In a funhouse mirror nothing is invented: it's your face, stretched tall or squashed wide. A misleading graph works the same way. The values are real, but cutting the axis at 86% stretches a 4-point gap into a towering difference, and doubling a picture's height and width makes 2 times look like 4. To see the real you, step back to a flat mirror: read the actual numbers and redraw from 0 in your head.

blocks.text: When an axis doesn't start at 0, ignore how tall the bars look and subtract or divide the actual values.

explain.body: Line: change over time. Bar: compare separate categories. Pie: parts of one whole. Histogram: spread of one numeric variable. Scatterplot: relationship between two numeric variables.

test.q: Which display best compares the number of applicants to the nursing programs at five different colleges this year?
test.why: Five colleges are separate categories, and comparing a count across categories is the job of a bar graph.

whyNot.1: A line graph shows change over time; the colleges are not a time sequence.
whyNot.2: A scatterplot needs two numeric variables per individual; here there is one count per college.
whyNot.3: A histogram groups one numeric variable into intervals; colleges are categories, not intervals.

explain.body: When the vertical axis starts above 0, each bar's visible height is its value minus the starting value. Small real differences then look huge. Always compare the actual values.

test.q: A bar graph's vertical axis starts at 60 instead of 0. One bar shows 90 and the other shows 70. Which statement is correct?
options: The 90 bar looks 1.3 times as tall
The 90 bar looks 1.5 times as tall
The bars look as they would from 0
The 90 bar looks 3 times as tall
test.why: Visible heights: 90 − 60 = 30 and 70 − 60 = 10. The 90 bar looks 30 ÷ 10 = 3 times as tall, although 90 is only about 1.3 times 70.

whyNot.0: 1.3 (90 ÷ 70) is how the bars would compare on an axis starting at 0.
whyNot.1: 1.5 divides 90 by the axis start, 60, which is not a bar height.
whyNot.2: Starting the axis at 60 changes the visible heights, so the bars look very different from a 0-based graph.

explain.body: Scaling a picture by k in height AND width multiplies its area by k × k. Equally spaced axis labels must stand for equal steps; if they don't, the slopes lie.

test.q: A health poster shows a syringe picture for last year's vaccinations. This year vaccinations tripled, so the artist tripled both the height and the width of the syringe. The new picture's area is how many times the original?
test.why: Area scales with height × width: 3 × 3 = 9 times, so a tripling looks like a nine-fold jump.

whyNot.0: 3 times would be correct only if one dimension had been tripled.
whyNot.1: 6 adds the two scale factors (3 + 3) instead of multiplying them.
whyNot.3: 27 is 3 × 3 × 3, the scale for volume, but a flat picture has only two dimensions.

explain.body: A graph can show accurate numbers for a hand-picked stretch of time that tells the opposite story from the full record. Ask what happened before and after the window shown.

test.q: A pharmacy's monthly prescriptions fell from 1,250 in January to 1,100 in July, rose to 1,320 in September, and ended at 1,200 in December. An ad graphs only July to September. What percent change does the ad show, and what was the change from January to December?

whyNot.0: 16.7% divides the rise of 220 by the new value, 1,320, instead of the starting value, 1,100.
whyNot.2: Prescriptions ended lower than they began (1,200 vs 1,250), so the year was down, not up.
whyNot.3: 4.2% divides the drop of 50 by the new value, 1,200, instead of the starting value, 1,250.
